answer_text:
The coefficient is
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n+1}{2}\right\rceil = 1,1,2,2,3,3,\dots
\]
so we can group terms in pairs:
\[
g(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (k+1)\left(x^{2k}+x^{2k+1}\right)
=(1+x)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)(x^2)^k.
\]

Using
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)y^k=\frac{1}{(1-y)^2},
\]
with \(y=x^2\), we get
\[
g(x)=\frac{1+x}{(1-x^2)^2}.
\]

Now simplify:
\[
(1-x^2)^2=(1-x)^2(1+x)^2,
\]
so
\[
g(x)=\frac{1+x}{(1-x)^2(1+x)^2}
=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2(1+x)}.
\]

Expanding the denominator:
\[
(1-x)^2(1+x)=1-x-x^2+x^3=x^3-x^2-x+1.
\]

Thus, for \(|x|<1\),
\[
g(x)=\frac{1}{x^3-x^2-x+1}.
\]

Now evaluate at \(x=\frac13\):
\[
g\left(\frac13\right)
=\frac{1}{\left(\frac13\right)^3-\left(\frac13\right)^2-\frac13+1}
=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{3}+1}.
\]
\[
=\frac{1}{\frac{1-3-9+27}{27}}
=\frac{1}{\frac{16}{27}}
=\frac{27}{16}.
\]

\[
\boxed{g\left(\frac13\right)=\frac{27}{16}\text{, and }g(x)=\frac{1}{x^3-x^2-x+1}\text{ for }|x|<1}
\]
